name: Myanmar civil war
started: 2021-02-01 (coup; current phase is the junta counteroffensive under a post-election government, 2025-2026)
summary: Five years after the 2021 coup, Myanmar's war has swung back toward the military on several fronts. With China having pushed the strongest northern ethnic armies into ceasefires, the junta, now presented as an elected government under President Min Aung Hlaing, is using air power, drones and river and sea lift to relieve besieged garrisons and retake towns, while the Arakan Army still holds most of Rakhine State.

sides.name: Myanmar military (Tatmadaw) and post-election government
backers: Russia (five-year military cooperation agreement signed 3 Feb 2026)
China (political ties; brokered ceasefires that took northern ethnic armies out of the fight)
leaders: Min Aung Hlaing (President from 3 Apr 2026; commander-in-chief until 30 Mar 2026)
sides.strength: No reliable public troop figure retrieved; stable control estimated at 72 to 220 of 330 townships (Wikipedia compilation, 2025-26), but holds most major cities.

sides.name: Arakan Army (AA)
members: AA-led resistance forces in Bago, Magway and Ayeyarwady regions
sides.strength: No independent figure retrieved; controls 14 of 17 Rakhine townships plus Paletwa in Chin State (DMG/BNI, Oct 2025; DVB, Feb 2026).

sides.name: Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and allied PDFs
NUG, People's Defence Forces and allied ethnic organisations
members: National Unity Government and People's Defence Forces
Kachin Independence Organisation (political wing of KIA)
leaders: Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF, formed 30 Mar 2026 by CRPH, NUG, KIO, KNU, KNPP, CNF)
sides.strength: No reliable figure; ACLED counts more than 1,200 active armed groups in Myanmar (NYT/ACLED, Jun 2026).

sides.name: Northern ethnic armies under China-brokered ceasefires
sides.strength: Out of the anti-junta coalition after Beijing-brokered ceasefires; MNDAA withdrew from Lashio and TNLA from Mogok and Mongmit.

background: The military seized power on 1 February 2021 and crushed street protests, which pushed opponents into armed resistance alongside long-established ethnic armies. In late 2023 a northern alliance (MNDAA, TNLA, AA) launched Operation 1027 and over the following year resistance forces captured dozens of towns, including the Northeastern Command at Lashio, and the AA took most of Rakhine. By 1 December 2025 anti-junta forces had captured 96 towns, 15 of them district-level or higher.

The tide turned in 2025. China, worried about its border trade, pipelines and the Kyaukphyu port project, pressured the MNDAA to hand back Lashio and the TNLA to withdraw from Mogok and Mongmit. The junta dissolved its State Administration Council on 31 July 2025, ran a three-phase election from December 2025 to January 2026 that observers called neither free nor fair, and installed Min Aung Hlaing as president in April 2026. This matters because the 'civilian' label is meant to win back foreign engagement (the United States opened direct talks in October 2026) without changing who holds military power.
year: Late 2025: the junta followed up its recapture of Kyaukme in northern Shan with offensives elsewhere, while the AA, which had pressed to within about 7 miles of Kyaukphyu, fell back to about 13 miles from the town under combined army, navy and air attack (DMG/BNI). The KNLA captured the Thai border trade town of Mawtaung in Tanintharyi on 14 November 2025. A December 2025 air strike on a hospital in Rakhine killed at least 30 people (Reuters). Voting took place on 28 December, 11 January and 25 January, with KIA-held Kachin townships excluded.

January to April 2026: the KIA resumed attacks on Bhamo on 14 January after a two-week pause and reportedly took Transport Battalion 933 east of the town, while the junta prepared a counteroffensive in Khaunglanhpu and Tsawlaw. The AA attacked the Danyawaddy naval base near Kyaukphyu and on 28 January seized the Point 666 outpost in Pandaung, Bago Region, which guards four military weapons factories. Air strikes killed at least 21 at Hteelin near Bhamo (22 January), 17 at Yoengu in Ponnagyun (24 February), 25 at a trading post in Mindon (1 March) and about 116 AA-held prisoners of war at a prison in Ann Township (8 March). The junta retook Tagaung, the last NUG-held town in Mandalay Region, on 13 March. Parliament convened on 16 March, Ye Win Oo became commander-in-chief on 30 March and Min Aung Hlaing was elected president on 3 April. The same day opposition bodies formed the SCEF to coordinate a federal alternative.

May to October 2026: under Ye Win Oo the junta retook at least five towns by late May, including Mawtaung on 19 May after a 15-day, three-column counteroffensive that sent 4,000 people fleeing into the hills and toward Thailand. A blast at an explosives store in Namhkam killed more than 46 people on 31 May. Amnesties freed thousands, ex-president Win Myint was released and Aung San Suu Kyi's sentence was commuted to house arrest. On 28 September an air strike on Kyauktaw town in Rakhine killed 50 and wounded at least 58, the deadliest in the state since the December hospital bombing. On 8 October the United States began direct negotiations with the military government.
situation: As of late October 2026 the military holds the centre, the main cities and the Bago-Mandalay corridor and is on the offensive against isolated resistance-held towns, with the dry season (November to April) about to open the best campaigning months. The AA controls almost all of Rakhine except Sittwe, Kyaukphyu and Manaung and is fighting in neighbouring Bago and Magway. The KIA's siege of Bhamo, now nearly two years old, is a grinding stalemate. The northern Shan front is largely quiet under Chinese-brokered ceasefires. Civilian deaths from air strikes remain the war's signature harm.
technical: Command change: Ye Win Oo succeeded Min Aung Hlaing as Commander-in-Chief on 30 Mar 2026; the junta retook at least five towns in the following two months (Wikipedia; Khaosod English).

Riverine lift at Bhamo: about 20 vessels sailed up the Ayeyarwady in two convoys (17 and 22 Jul 2025) and a Navy fleet arrived 1 Aug 2025 with troops, artillery and drones; the junta then regained Artillery Battalion 366 and half of Bhamo airport on 10 Aug 2025 (BNI/KNG; DVB).
KIA withdrew from Tank Battalion 5014 and LIB 236 on 11 Sep 2025 but took an outpost guarding Infantry Battalion 47 on 29 Sep 2025 and positions on a two-mile stretch of the Bhamo-Momauk road (DVB).

KIA renewed attacks on Bhamo on 14 Jan 2026 and reportedly captured Transport Battalion 933 about 8 km east of the town; the Air Force answered with retaliatory strikes; IB 46 sent 200+ troops to Khaunglanhpu (DVB, unverified KIA claims).

Kyaukphyu: junta used combined army, navy and air operations, sea-lifted reinforcements, drone bombing and naval gunfire; AA fell back from about 7 to about 13 miles from town by end-Sep 2025 (DMG via BNI).
AA has attacked Danyawaddy naval base about 30 km east of Kyaukphyu since Jan 2026; about 400 junta reinforcements reached LID 34 in late Jan 2026 (DVB).

Defence-industrial targeting: Pandaung (Bago) hosts four DDI (KaPaSa) weapons factories; AA took Point 666 there on 28 Jan 2026 after a three-month siege. Ngape (Magway) hosts DDI 14, reported to make air-defence missiles; AA-led forces have surrounded its Natyaykan air defence base since Oct 2025 (DVB).

Light aviation for strikes: two gyrocopters launched from the Northwest Regional Military Command, escorted by an Mi-35P helicopter firing machine guns, hit a workshop in Ye-U Township on 7 September, killing seven; same-day gyrocopter strikes in Chaung-U Township (BNI, year not stated in article).

Mawtaung counteroffensive (May 2026): 50-truck convoy staged at Thebyu about 41 km away, then three columns encircled the town backed by artillery and air strikes; state media claimed 200+ clashes in 15 days and at least 24 opposition fighters killed (Khaosod English).
Air strike lethality 2026: Ann Township prison strike (8 Mar) killed about 116 AA prisoners of war; Kyauktaw strike (28 Sep) killed 50 and wounded 58+ (Wikipedia; Reuters).
Martial law was imposed on 63 townships on 29 Jul 2025 when the nationwide state of emergency was lifted ahead of the election (DVB).

China's leverage: MNDAA withdrew from Lashio and TNLA from Mogok and Mongmit; Beijing-brokered ceasefires took two northern armies out of the anti-junta coalition (Wikipedia; Khaosod English). China executed 15 members of the Ming and Bai scam-centre families of Laukkai in Jan-Feb 2026 (Wikipedia).
Russia: five-year military cooperation agreement signed 3 Feb 2026 (Wikipedia).
Fragmentation: ACLED counts more than 1,200 active armed groups and rated Myanmar the most extreme conflict of 2025 apart from the Palestinian territories (NYT/ACLED, Jun 2026).
casualties: About 89,200 to 96,000+ killed since 2021 (ACLED, 1 Jan 2026); around 100,000 killed (Reuters, 29 Sep 2026). Notable 2026 air strikes: Hteelin 21+, Yoengu 17+, Mindon 25+, Bago offensive 30+, Ann prison about 116, Kyauktaw 50 (Wikipedia 2026 in Myanmar; Reuters). Military and resistance combat losses are not reliably reported; figures from either side are unverified.
displaced: Over 3.5 million displaced (Reuters, 29 Sep 2026); about 299,000 refugees in neighbouring countries (UNHCR, May 2026). At least 4,000 fled Mawtaung in May 2026 (Khaosod English).

timeline.event: KNU/KNLA captures Mawtaung, a Thai border trade town in Tanintharyi.
First phase of junta-run general election.
KIA resumes attacks on Bhamo; reportedly captures Transport Battalion 933.
AA seizes Point 666 outpost in Pandaung, Bago Region, after three-month siege.
Myanmar and Russia sign five-year military cooperation agreement.
Air strike on a prison in Ann Township kills about 116 AA prisoners of war.
Junta retakes Tagaung, last NUG-held town in Mandalay Region.
Ye Win Oo becomes Commander-in-Chief; opposition forms SCEF.
Parliament elects Min Aung Hlaing president.
Aung San Suu Kyi's remaining sentence commuted to house arrest.
Explosion at explosives store in Namhkam, Shan State, kills 46+.
Air strike on Kyauktaw, Rakhine, kills 50.
United States begins direct negotiations with the military government.

outlook: The November to April dry season favours the military's ground and air operations; watch for junta pushes to break the Bhamo siege and clear AA forces from around Kyaukphyu and Sittwe, and whether the AA escalates in Bago, Magway and Ayeyarwady. Whether US engagement and Chinese pressure produce talks with the KIA or AA, or simply legitimise the new government, is the key diplomatic question. Air strikes on markets, schools and prisons are likely to keep civilian deaths high.

battles.name: Air strike on Kyauktaw
battles.outcome: Strike on town; AA vowed retaliation.
battles.losses: 50 killed, at least 58 wounded, including women and children (aid worker via Reuters).
battles.significance: Deadliest strike in Rakhine since a December 2025 hospital bombing; the AA says markets, schools and homes were deliberately targeted, while the military says it exercises 'maximum restraint'.

sources.label: Daily Maverick/Reuters (29 Sep 2026)

battles.place: Tagaung, Thabeikkyin District, Mandalay Region, Myanmar
battles.outcome: Military retook the last NUG-held town in Mandalay Region.
battles.significance: Removed the resistance's last town foothold in Mandalay Region, the military's heartland.

battles.name: Air strike on prison in Ann Township
sides: Arakan Army (prison holding AA prisoners of war)
battles.outcome: Prison hit; about 116 AA prisoners of war killed.
battles.forces: Myanmar Air Force strike aircraft (type not reported).
battles.significance: One of the deadliest single strikes of the year in Myanmar; it shows the air force can hit AA rear areas at will, and that prisoners held by the AA are themselves exposed to junta bombing.

battles.place: Hteelin, Bhamo Township, Kachin State, Myanmar (approximate location)
battles.outcome: Village struck during renewed Bhamo fighting.
battles.significance: Came a week after the KIA renewed its Bhamo offensive, illustrating the junta's use of air strikes on surrounding communities.

battles.name: Battle of Mawtaung
battles.place: Mawtaung (Mawdaung / Singkhon Pass), Tanintharyi Region, Myanmar
battles.outcome: KNLA captured the town on 14 Nov 2025; the military retook it on 19 May 2026 after a 15-day counteroffensive.
battles.forces: Junta: 50-truck convoy staged at Thebyu, three encircling columns with artillery and air strikes. KNLA withdrew citing firepower.
battles.losses: State media claimed at least 24 opposition fighters killed and acknowledged unnumbered military deaths; 4,000+ residents of Mawtaung and nine villages fled (Khaosod English).
battles.significance: Mawtaung is a Thai border trade gate; its recapture was one of at least five towns retaken after Ye Win Oo took command, signalling a junta offensive in the south.

battles.name: Siege of Point 666, Pandaung
battles.outcome: AA seized the Point 666 outpost after a three-month siege; junta answered with air strikes on 29-30 Jan 2026.
battles.forces: AA-led forces vs junta garrison guarding four DDI (KaPaSa) weapons factories.
battles.losses: At least 100 junta troops killed over three months per a source cited by DVB; AA losses undisclosed.
battles.significance: Puts the AA in reach of the military's own arms factories outside Rakhine, showing it can project force into the Bago-Magway heartland.

battles.name: Siege of Natyaykan air defence base
sides: Arakan Army and allied resistance forces
battles.outcome: Base surrounded; AA captured all outposts in Gokkyi and Suntat villages; junta relief column and air strikes on nearby villages (as of Feb 2026).
battles.forces: AA-led forces vs air defence base guarding DDI 14, reportedly a factory for air-defence missiles.
battles.significance: A threat to one of the few factories producing air-defence missiles for the military.

sources.label: DVB: Arakan Army attacks regime forces in Rakhine, Bago and Magway (2 Feb 2026)

battles.name: Battle for Kyaukphyu and Danyawaddy naval base
battles.outcome: Junta counteroffensive pushed the AA back from about 7 to about 13 miles from town by end-Sep 2025; AA attacks on Danyawaddy naval base continued from Jan 2026; town remains junta-held.
battles.forces: Junta LID 34 (about 400 reinforcements late Jan 2026), Police Battalion 32, Danyawaddy naval base, warships providing gunfire, drones and aircraft vs AA.
battles.losses: Unverified AA claims of hundreds of junta dead, mostly conscripts (DMG via BNI).
battles.significance: Kyaukphyu is the terminus of China's oil and gas pipelines and the site of a planned special economic zone and deep-sea port; holding it keeps Beijing invested in the junta and denies the AA full control of Rakhine.

sources.label: BNI/DMG: AA withdraws in parts of Kyaukphyu (28 Oct 2025)
DVB: Arakan Army attacks regime forces (2 Feb 2026)

battles.name: Siege of Bhamo
sides: Kachin Independence Army and allied PDFs
battles.outcome: Ongoing stalemate. Junta riverine reinforcement in Jul-Aug 2025 retook Artillery Battalion 366 and half the airport; KIA renewed attacks 14 Jan 2026 and reportedly took Transport Battalion 933.
battles.forces: KIA and PDF units vs junta MOC 21, IB 47, IB 236/LIB 236, Tank Battalion 5014, Artillery Battalion 366, reinforced by a Navy flotilla of about 20 vessels; heavy junta air and suicide-drone use.
battles.losses: No reliable totals; air strike at Hteelin, Bhamo Township killed at least 21 on 22 Jan 2026 (Wikipedia). Most homes in Bhamo destroyed by air and drone strikes (DVB).
battles.significance: Bhamo is Kachin State's second city and the gateway to the China border trade road; its fall would be the KIA's biggest prize, and its survival shows how river lift and air power let the junta hold isolated garrisons.
